passage:
Harsha,

I've been angry for a week, and I want to write this before I say something I'll regret.

You forgot my graduation dinner. I kept a chair for you all evening. I told myself you just don't care, that you've never cared, that I've been the only one trying.

And then I remembered last winter. When I had dengue, you drove four hours from Nashik, slept on my floor for three nights and made me that terrible khichdi.

Both of those are you. The friend who drove four hours, and the friend who forgot the dinner. I don't have to pick one. You can be caring and careless. So can I, honestly.

I'm still a bit hurt. But I'm not going to throw away the four hours because of one missed dinner.

Coffee on Sunday?

Kamal

qa.q: How far did Harsha drive when Kamal had dengue?
qa.a: Four hours, from Nashik.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel after remembering last winter?
qa.a: Kamal still felt hurt, but remembering Harsha's care made the anger less explosive and the disappointment easier to hold.

qa.q: What makes Kamal's letter a steadier way to handle disappointment?
qa.a: It names the hurt honestly while keeping Harsha's caring side in view, so the friendship isn't thrown away over one mistake.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Harsha might feel guilty about the dinner but also relieved and grateful that Kamal still sees the whole friendship.

grounding: Shows an adult telling themselves that a friend can be caring and careless, keeping both in view so the disappointment is less explosive.

passage: Nandini, you asked how I stopped fighting with my mother every week. Let me, Sahil, explain. For years I saw her in two ways. When she was kind, she was a saint. When she forgot something, she was the worst mother alive. Like the night she forgot to pick me up from the station at midnight, and I waited two hours. I didn't speak to her for a week. But the same woman sat by my bed for eleven nights when I had typhoid in class nine, wiping my forehead. Both are true. She's caring and she's careless. Once I let myself hold both, something changed. When she forgets now, I'm annoyed, and I tell her. But it doesn't feel like the end of the world. It's just her careless side. Her caring side is still there, right next to it.

qa.q: How long did Sahil wait at the station?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: Why does Sahil feel less upset now when his mother forgets something?
qa.a: Sahil holds both her careless and caring sides in mind, so a lapse feels annoying, not like a betrayal that erases everything good.

qa.q: What could Nandini take from Sahil's story for her own relationships?
qa.a: That she can admit someone's flaws and their care together, and speak up about the flaw without deciding the whole person is bad.

qa.q: How might Sahil's mother experience the change in him?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and closer to him, hearing honest complaints instead of weeks of silence.

grounding: Shows an adult learning to see a parent as both caring and careless, making the relationship steadier and disappointment less explosive.

passage: I share a flat with Ayesha in Hyderabad, and I saw how she handled Chinmay missing her award ceremony. I can only say what I saw. He'd promised to come. The seat next to her stayed empty. She came home with the trophy, sat on the sofa, and was quiet for a long time. I expected her to call him and end it. She'd done that before, with others. Instead she said, half to me and half to herself, "He's the one who stayed up all night helping me with the application. He's also the one who forgot tonight. Both are Chinmay." Then she called him. I heard her say, calmly, "I'm really hurt you weren't there. I needed you tonight." She didn't shout. She didn't say it was over. The next morning, he turned up with breakfast and an apology.

qa.q: What did Chinmay help Ayesha with?
qa.a: He stayed up all night helping her with the application.

qa.q: Why didn't Ayesha end things with Chinmay, as the narrator expected?
qa.a: Ayesha felt hurt and disappointed, but holding in mind both his help with the application and his forgetfulness kept the disappointment from exploding.

qa.q: What makes Ayesha's phone call a good response?
qa.a: She named her hurt clearly and calmly, without shouting or ending things, which invited Chinmay to take responsibility.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt hearing Ayesha's calm words?
qa.a: Chinmay likely felt guilty and grateful for the chance to make it right, which is why he came with breakfast and an apology.

grounding: Shows, through a flatmate's account, an adult holding that her partner is both caring and careless, keeping disappointment steady.

Ishita looked up from her marking. Omkar stood on a chair in her flip-flops, holding a ruler.

Today at dress-up Dolma chose her father's old boots, which he'd sent for the box. She clomped to the chairs we'd lined up as a bus. "I'm Papa. I drive the big bus." She turned an imaginary wheel and called out, "Hold tight, sharp turn!" in a deep voice. Sachin sat behind her as a passenger. When he stood up, she said sternly, "Sit down, please. Safety first," which I'm told her father says. She looked so proud. What I did next: I gave her a paper ticket book, and she spent the rest of the hour collecting tickets.

passage:
Coach's note, under-twelve girls' cricket, Pune.
Since the national series on TV, Shalini, eleven, has turned herself into a copy of the star opener Kaveri Bose. The red headband. The high backlift. The way she taps her bat twice. Her batting has actually improved; she stands taller, braver. But she's also copied the glare. Today, after hitting a four, she stared down Sabina, the bowler, and said, "Is that all you've got?" Sabina's face fell. What I did next: I sat Shalini down and told her I love the headband and the backlift. Then I asked, "What does Kaveri do after a match?" She thought. "She shakes hands with everyone." "So take that from her too." Shalini nodded. At the end of practice, she shook Sabina's hand.

qa.q: Who is Shalini copying?
qa.a: The star opener Kaveri Bose.

qa.q: Why does Shalini stand taller when she copies Kaveri Bose?
qa.a: Copying her hero makes Shalini feel braver and stronger, as if she has some of Kaveri's power.

qa.q: What did the coach do well?
qa.a: The coach praised what was good, then pointed Shalini to her hero's sportsmanship, helping her drop the swagger without shaming her.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Shalini glared at her?
qa.a: Sabina probably felt hurt and small, taunted after being hit for four.

grounding: Shows a child copying a cricketer's stance and attitude, feeling some of the hero's strength, while also importing swagger.

I have decided I am going to be exactly like Veer Shetty, the kabaddi raider on TV. I cut my fringe short like his. I practise his crouch in the corridor. And I say, "Come on then!" before every raid, like he does, with my chin up.

I don't think it looked silly. He's the best.

passage:
Diary. Hrithik.

Last year they called me "Tuh-tuh-Tiger" because of my stammer. Every single day. I used to eat lunch in the toilet.

Today a new boy joined, Sonam, from Sikkim. He has an accent. When he said "vegetable" wrong, I copied him really loudly. Everyone laughed. At me, WITH me. First time. I felt big. Safe.

Then Pallavi said, just to me, "That's exactly what they did to you." I didn't answer.

After lunch Mrs Pinto called me in. She'd heard. She didn't shout. She asked me how it felt last year. I told her about the toilet. Then she asked how Sonam might feel. She's calling both our parents today and wants Sonam and me to talk tomorrow with her there.

I don't feel big now. I feel sick. I did the same thing to him.

qa.q: What did Hrithik eat lunch in last year?
qa.a: In the toilet.

qa.q: Why did mocking Sonam make Hrithik feel big and safe at first?
qa.a: After being the target last year, being on the laughing side felt powerful and protective, like escaping the victim role.

qa.q: What was right about Mrs Pinto's response?
qa.a: She acted the same day, helped Hrithik connect last year's pain to Sonam's, called both families, and set up a supported talk.

qa.q: How might Sonam have felt being copied loudly on his first day?
qa.a: Sonam likely felt humiliated and alone, much as Hrithik had felt the year before.

grounding: Shows a teenager who was bullied beginning to mock a weaker student, taking the powerful role and repeating the harm, and an adult stepping in the same day.

passage:
Diary, Thursday. Rajni.

Six weeks as a trainee at the newspaper and I've realised I've turned into a mini-Kunal. I say "Let's cut the fluff" in every meeting. I tap my pen twice before I speak, like he does. I even say "Right, right, right" when someone's talking. The funny thing is, it works. People listen more. I feel less like a kid pretending.

Today in the edit meeting I said "Let's cut the fluff" and my colleague Neha laughed and said, "Okay, Kunal." I laughed too, but it stung a bit.

So tonight I've been thinking. The pen-tap is useful; it makes me pause. "Cut the fluff" isn't really me; I like fluff. And "right, right, right" makes me sound like I'm not listening.

Tomorrow, I'll keep the pause. And try saying something in my own words.

qa.q: What phrase does Rajni say in every meeting?
qa.a: "Let's cut the fluff."

qa.q: Why did Neha's comment sting?
qa.a: Rajni felt embarrassed to realise how much of Kunal's style had been copied, and wondered what was really Rajni's own.

qa.q: What makes Rajni's plan for tomorrow a good one?
qa.a: Keeping the pen-tap pause that helps and dropping the phrases that don't fit is a way to test what truly suits, moving toward a personal style.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel if he noticed Rajni copying him?
qa.a: Kunal might feel flattered and amused, and perhaps glad that Rajni is growing more confident.

grounding: Shows a young trainee using a senior's phrases and habits to feel confident and later testing what genuinely fits.

passage: At the government school in a village near Kolar, Salma had been a trainee teacher for two months, learning from Kiran madam, who had taught there for twenty years. Salma now started every class the way Kiran madam did: "Eyes on me, champions!" She clapped three times for silence. She even put her hand on her hip the same way. The children responded instantly. Salma felt taller. But one morning she said "champions" and it sounded strange in her mouth, like wearing someone else's sandals. Later, over tea, she told Kiran madam. The older teacher laughed. "I copied my headmistress for years. Then one day I said 'champions' by accident, and it stuck. Try your own words sometimes. See what fits." The next day, Salma tried: "Good morning, my stars." The children giggled, then looked up. She kept the claps.

qa.q: How many times does Salma clap for silence?

March: At the Surat textile firm, Jagdish, twenty-six and newly a supervisor, looked at Manjula's order sheet. "Is this the best you can do? A child could do better." He heard it as he said it: his father's exact voice, the same words his father had used over his homework for years. Manjula went pale. Jagdish went home shaken.
April: That month, Jagdish wrote two lists in a notebook. From his father, keep: checks everything twice, never late, finishes what he starts. Drop: sharp words, never saying well done.
June: Manjula brought him a sheet with three errors. Jagdish felt the old words rise. He paused. "Good layout. Three things to fix here. Walk me through how you checked it?" She relaxed and found two errors herself. At the end he said, "Well done." It felt strange. It felt like his own voice.

qa.q: What did Jagdish say to Manjula in March?
qa.a: "Is this the best you can do? A child could do better."

qa.q: Why did Jagdish go home shaken in March?
qa.a: He was upset to hear his father's harsh voice in his own mouth, and saw how it hurt Manjula the way it had hurt him.

qa.q: How did Jagdish's two lists help him?
qa.a: They let him deliberately keep his father's diligence and drop the sharpness, turning an inherited pattern into a choice.

qa.q: How might Manjula experience Jagdish's June feedback compared to March?
qa.a: Manjula probably felt respected and calmer in June, able to find errors herself instead of feeling humiliated.

passage: I'm Arnab. When I was fifteen, I shouted at Baba because he said I couldn't go to the late-night concert. I said he was a dictator. I slammed my door so hard the picture fell. The next morning I felt awful. So I got up at six, swept the whole flat, washed the dishes, watered Ma's plants and made Baba's tea exactly how he likes it, two sugars. I didn't say a word. My little brother Ojas watched me with his mouth open. "Why are you being so weird?" Baba drank his tea, looked at the shining floor, and didn't say much either. All day he was quiet. That evening he said, "The tea was very good. But I'm still waiting for you to tell me what you're sorry for." That was the hardest sentence I'd ever heard. Then I said it.

qa.a: Arnab felt guilty about shouting and calling Baba a dictator, and hoped the actions would show sorry without having to say it.

qa.a: That actions can show guilt, but the person who was hurt may still need to hear what the apology is for.
